A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Benign Overfitting in Token Selection of Attention Mechanism. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial reformatting and appendix renumbering.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original synthetic experiments and classification experiments using ViT and BERT on six datasets. Appendix G includes an additional synthetic loss heatmap.

after.justification: The original empirical results remain, and Appendix F adds transformer-encoder experiments, label-noise sensitivity results and measurements of attention dynamics on real datasets.

M1.justification: The analyzed model remains single-layer attention with a fixed classifier head and gradient descent on W and p using binary cross-entropy. The added encoder experiments and head-gradient proposition extend evaluation and theoretical justification without changing this procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic classification distribution and MNIST, CIFAR-10, PneumoniaMNIST, BreastMNIST, AG-news and TREC. The additions vary model configuration and training-label corruption within this retained dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix F.1 adds a one-layer transformer encoder as an architectural comparator, explicitly comparing its attention trajectories and loss heatmaps with the analyzed model. The additional Magen et al. row in Table 1 is a literature comparison, not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: The original experimental settings remain. New protocols include joint optimization of the encoder, real-data controls at label-noise levels 0 and 0.2, a noise sweep with training size 200, and tracking maximum CLS-token attention. These supplement the existing experiments rather than replace Table 2's protocol.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained synthetic attention trajectories and SNR heatmap, v3 tests architectural sensitivity through the encoder experiments, sensitivity to label-noise severity through Table 6 and Figure 8, and attention concentration on real datasets through Figure 9. These substantially broaden the diagnostic analyses.

E5.justification: Table 2 reports means and standard deviations over three runs in both versions. New Table 6 follows the same practice; no changed run counts, seed-reporting practice, confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: Table 2, Figure 3 and the original synthetic heatmap remain unchanged. New Table 6 reports, for example, AG-news accuracy at n=1000 of 85.5±0.3 with no label noise and 69.6±1.1 with noise 0.2. Figures 6–9 add encoder, noise-sensitivity and attention findings. These are results under added conditions, not same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: Section 3.5 revises assumptions A1–A4 and A8, including changing A1's signal-norm exponent from 3/2 to 4/3. The signed head condition becomes k cos(theta_k)>Theta(1), and Theorem 4.1's non-overfitting time gains a denominator factor d, with corresponding proof revisions. Remark 4.8 adds a rho-dependent timescale qualification, and Appendix E.2 adds Proposition E.1 and its head-gradient geometry proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution paragraphs and conclusion retain the central claims: SNR-dependent benign overfitting can arise solely through token selection, and generalization can follow fitting after a substantial delay. The added analyses support and qualify these existing claims.

C2.justification: Appendix E.2 newly discusses why training the head on the same samples invalidates an independence argument and how separate data changes that situation. Appendix F interprets encoder behavior through capacity, learnable token scores and distributed noise memorization, and explicitly discusses real-data attention patterns and architectural differences outside the analytical setting.

D1.justification: The added experiments document the encoder's single-head attention, nonlinear feedforward layers, normalization and skip connections, and specify the CLS-attention readout and noise-sweep setup. Existing pretrained-model dimensions, optimizer settings, separate head-pretraining data and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds Papyan et al. (2020), removes Yun et al. (2020), and includes already-cited Magen et al. (2024) in Table 1. Appendix A revises the Magen comparison, removing the two-token characterization and adding discussion of experimental validation, while retaining the broader research positioning.

P1.justification: v3 substantially expands the explanatory narrative around the fixed head and proof techniques, adds an appendix contents list and proof roadmap, and extensively edits proof prose. It also consolidates high-probability events into the preliminaries and groups the multiclass extension with further discussion.

P2.justification: The main text and references adopt a two-column conference layout with running headers. Figure 1 gains explicit SNR annotations; v3 adds the proof illustration in Figure 4, experimental Figures 6–9 and two-panel Table 6. Original Figures 2–3 and the heatmap, renumbered from Figure 4 to Figure 5, are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves the justification and assessability of the central analysis through the corrected head-alignment condition, revised mathematical bounds, an idealized head-alignment derivation with explicit limitations, and a proof roadmap. Added noise controls, encoder comparisons and real-attention diagnostics address gaps in v2's connection between theory and practical behavior. The gains concern better-supported and more clearly bounded conclusions; the original benchmark scores remain unchanged.
